newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma Gov. hopes truth will come out at trial.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma Gov. hopes truth will come out at trial.

text.p: The governor of Oklahoma said on Sunday he hoped the "truth will come out" in the trial of accused Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh, which is set to begin this week.

McVeigh, 28, a disgruntled Gulf War veteran, goes on trial on Monday charged with the April 19, 1995 truck bombing that destroyed the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in Oklahoma City, killing 168 people and injuring more than 500.

U.S. District Judge Richard Matsch and attorneys must first select 12 impartial jurors and six alternates to sit in judgment over McVeigh, who could be sentenced to death if found guilty of the worst bomb attack on U.S. soil.
"Hopefully the truth will come out, because that's all we want," Oklahoma Gov. Frank Keating said on NBC's "Meet the Press" on Sunday.

"Oklahoma has no interest in convicting innocent people. Because of the horrific nature of this event we want the right people identified, the right people tried, convicted and executed. We hope these are the people," the Republican governor said.

Prosecutors allege McVeigh and former army buddy Terry Nichols, who they say shared extreme right-wing, anti-government views, used a rented truck packed with fertiliser and fuel oil to bomb the federal building.

They say they wanted to avenge the raid by federal agents on the Branch Davidian sect's compound at Waco, Texas, which led to the deaths of about 80 people on April 19, 1993 -- exactly two years before the Oklahoma City blast. Both men have pleaded not guilty. Nichols will be tried later.
In the federal court trial, expected to last up to four months, McVeigh is charged with planting the bomb and with the first-degree murder of eight federal officials killed in the blast.
Legal experts expect prosecutors to base their case against McVeigh on extensive physical evidence as well as records and witnesses to show he rented the truck used in the bombing.

McVeigh's lawyers say he is innocent. In a court filing last week, they suggested a foreign country, probably Iraq, may have planned the attack, recruiting American neo-Nazis to carry out the bombing.

The federal courthouse in Denver -- where the trial was moved because of concerns McVeigh could not receive a fair trial in Oklahoma City -- has been turned into a fortress. Concrete barriers ring the building and surveillance cameras scan the outside.
Twelve seats for victims have been set aside in the Denver courtroom. Other victims and relatives will watch proceedings in Oklahoma City on closed-circuit television.

The trial will go ahead as scheduled despite protests from McVeigh's lawyers that he cannot get a fair trial because of news reports -- denied by lead defence attorney Stephen Jones -- that McVeigh confessed to his lawyers that he was responsible for the bombing.

In February Matsch sent surveys to 1,000 prospective jurors in Denver and 22 surrounding counties. About 500 prospective jurors were called to a meeting in March when they filled in a second questionnaire. Prospective jurors will be asked about their views and knowledge of the case this week as the jury pool is whittled down.
Jury selection is expected to take several weeks.
